passage:
At nine, Aditi fell out of the mango tree and came home with a cast on one arm. The pain faded, but the anger stayed: no cricket, no cycling, everyone else out in the lane. At night Aditi whispered, "What if it never works properly again?" Indu, Aditi's mother, answered honestly. "The doctor says it will heal, and it takes time. Let's mark one small thing each day." They drew a chart: buttoning a shirt, holding a pencil.

At twenty, a football injury to the knee brought a long slow recovery. Aditi did the exercises furiously, set the knee back, then skipped a week in a sulk, hating to ask flatmates to carry the bag. The physiotherapist said, "Steady and measured beats all or nothing," and Aditi settled into a modest daily routine.

At twenty-five, after a scooter collision at a junction, Aditi's body healed but Aditi jumped at every horn, took the long way round the junction and replayed the skid at night. Pallavi, a friend, walked to the junction with Aditi on Sundays and stopped whenever Aditi asked. When the jumpiness lingered, Aditi saw a counsellor, on Pallavi's suggestion.

qa.q: What did Indu suggest marking on the chart?
qa.a: Indu suggested marking one small thing each day, such as buttoning a shirt or holding a pencil.

qa.q: How does what troubles Aditi change from age nine to age twenty to age twenty-five, and what helps each time?
qa.a: At nine Aditi is angry and afraid the arm will never work properly, and small daily goals from Indu help; at twenty Aditi swings between overdoing and giving up, and a steady routine helps; at twenty-five the body has healed but fear of the junction remains, and Pallavi's company and a counsellor help.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when whispering, "What if it never works properly again?"
qa.a: Aditi was frightened and worried about the future, on top of the anger about missing play.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do next for Aditi?
qa.a: Pallavi can keep the Sunday walks going at Aditi's pace and keep encouraging the counsellor visits, without hurrying trust back.

grounding: A child with a fracture, a young adult with a slow-healing knee and a person after a road accident show injury affecting the mind, with steady support helping recovery.
